items.quote: The most High created this Fift Essence as the root of life in Nature for the preservation of the four qualities of the Humane body
items.note: Croll says God made the Fift Essence as the root of life in Nature, to preserve the four qualities of man's body; the sentence goes on to liken this to Heaven preserving the universe.

items.quote: The celestiall Fire that burneth not, is the soul and life of all Creatures
items.note: The text says what the celestiall Fire that does not burn is: the soul and life of all creatures.

items.quote: the Influences of all celestiall bodies which are communicated to the sublunary to every one in particular, these are concentred in this one
items.note: The influences that each thing below the moon receives singly from the heavenly bodies are said to be gathered together in this one subject.

items.quote: The Theater of the secrets of all Natur's Light
items.what: The Theater of the secrets of all Natur's Light
items.note: First of a run of names the text gives to the one thing it is speaking of.

items.quote: the Glasse of God's Mysteries, and the Miracle of universall Nature; the Fift Essence of the whole frame of the world, and the whole world Regenerated, wherein the Treasure of all Nature lyeth
items.what: the Glasse of God's Mysteries, and the Miracle of universall Nature; the Fift Essence of the whole frame of the world, and the whole world Regenerated
items.note: Further names for the same thing: a glass of God's mysteries, the Fift Essence of the whole world, the whole world regenerated.

items.quote: Subject and Instrument of all Naturall and Transnaturall Virtues
items.what: Subject and Instrument of all Naturall and Transnaturall Virtues
items.note: Another name in the run: it is both subject and instrument of virtues the text calls natural and transnatural.

items.quote: the Son of the Sun and Moon, who by his ascending into Heaven and descending into the Earth hath obtained all power of superior and inferior things
items.what: the Son of the Sun and Moon
items.note: The thing is named as a son of Sun and Moon and spoken of as 'who', a person that goes up to Heaven and down to Earth and so has power over things above and below.
items.term: Son of the Sun and Moon

items.quote: the Habitation of all metallick, minerall, and vegetable Forms, which God created under the Globe of the Moon
items.what: the Habitation of all metallick, minerall, and vegetable Forms
items.note: Another name in the run: the dwelling of all metallic, mineral and vegetable forms under the moon.

items.quote: it is truly the spirit of Life which pierceth through all other spirits
items.note: The text says the thing is truly the spirit of Life, which goes through all other spirits.

items.quote: is altogether one and the same with the spirit of our body, the bond between the Body and Soul
items.note: It is said to be one and the same with the spirit of our body, and that spirit is called the bond between body and soul.

items.quote: there is need of the Balsom of life as a means to be sought from Externalls, by which the internall is restored to retaine or sustaine the Fire of a long life
items.note: To make peace between soul and body a Balsom of life must be sought from outside, which restores the inward one; the sentence goes on to liken its lack to a lamp going out for want of oil.

items.quote: it is the most simple Matter which the Best and Greatest Lord generated out of the spirit of this world for the restauration and preservation of Humane Nature
items.note: The text says what the thing is as matter: the most simple matter, generated by God out of the spirit of this world, for restoring and preserving human nature.

items.quote: which hath been altogether unknown to the Physitians of our time
items.note: The matter is said to be wholly unknown to the physicians of the author's time.

items.quote: who goe not into the Temple of Apollo through the right door, but break through the Roofe, and sit in his seat, as the Scribes and Pharisees heretofore in Moses chair
items.note: Croll's charge against the Schools, put as a figure: they do not enter Apollo's temple by the right door but break in through the roof, and are likened to the Scribes and Pharisees in Moses' chair.

items.quote: while they hold the keys of Sciences in unrighteous captivity
items.note: The same men are said to keep the keys of the sciences captive; the sentence goes on to say they neither enter the 'Academy of Nature' themselves nor let others enter.

items.quote: others who desire to enter in a right way they hinder in their laudable course by their pernicious dehortations
items.note: They are said to hinder by dissuasion those who would enter the right way, so that these never come to know the truth.

items.quote: The life of natural things is the Union of the Ideall Light, as also with the Ideall of Heaven and Earth.
items.note: The margin note beside the opening of the paragraph states what the life of natural things is: a union of the 'Ideall Light' with the 'Ideall' of Heaven and Earth.

items.quote: By this Art the knowledge of almost all things, and in this Stone the universal Nature of things shineth forth.
items.note: The margin note beside the run of names speaks of 'this Art' and 'this Stone'; the lines of the paragraph itself that were given do not use the word Stone.

items.quote: The Tincture is the Fife Essence of the Microcosm
items.note: The margin note says what the Tincture is: the Fift Essence of the Microcosm (the note prints 'Fife').

items.quote: near to the first and most perfect Being and that Cabalisticall unary number
items.note: The note says the Tincture comes near to the first and most perfect Being and to a 'Cabalisticall unary number'.

items.quote: Paracelsus calleth it the perfect, perpetuall
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The margin note gives names for it to Paracelsus; the words that follow name it a Balsom of Physitians or Phylosophers (the word before 'Balsom' has letters the transcription could not read).

items.quote: the Defensive of old age, the Universall medicament, which like the invisible Fire consumeth all diseases
items.what: the Defensive of old age, the Universall medicament
items.note: Further names in the same note, standing in the sentence that begins 'Paracelsus calleth it'.

items.quote: Those Ancients who had most perfect knowledge of Things have called this Fist Essence the middle nature of Soules.
items.name: Those Ancients who had most perfect knowledge of Things
items.note: The margin note gives a name for the Fift Essence (printed 'Fist') to unnamed Ancients; it stands beside the words that call it the spirit of Life and the bond between body and soul.

items.quote: the true originall of all corporall diseases, in the judgement of the best Physitians, is the enormity of the Naturall proportion of the Three First
items.name: the best Physitians
items.note: The cause of bodily diseases, a disproportion of the 'Three First', is given as the judgement of 'the best Physitians'; Croll builds on it.

items.quote: as common Physitians say, the disorder and ill disposition of the four Elements or Humors
items.name: common Physitians
items.note: A second way of naming the same cause, given in a bracket to 'common Physitians': disorder of the four Elements or Humors.

items.quote: this foresaid Medicine, which is in it selfe the matter of our Creation may be congeneous and uniform to the substance, consisting in equality
items.note: The medicine spoken of before is said to be the matter of our creation and of one kind with 'the substance', its nature lying in equality.

items.quote: the Fift Essence or Fift Virtue resulting from the purer Essence of the four Elements, purified, incorruptible is compared to Heaven
items.note: The text gives a second name, Fift Virtue, and says where the Fift Essence comes from: the purer essence of the four Elements; it is likened to Heaven.

items.quote: nor doth it admit any malignant spirit, but they all fly from it
items.note: It is said to take in no malignant spirit; such spirits flee it.

items.quote: therefore it expelleth as much as is possible by Nature all accidentall corruptibility from which any sicknesse or weaknesse may arise
items.note: Because it is itself as little open to corruption as may be, it drives out corruptibility that comes by accident; the claim is limited by 'as much as is possible by Nature'.

items.quote: by reconciliation cureth againe the diseases that hapned by the exaltation of the Three Principles
items.note: It cures by reconciling; the diseases are said to come from the 'exaltation' of the Three Principles. The same paragraph earlier says 'Three First'.

items.quote: When the purified Elements are reduced to a pure and equall simplicity then is got the Medicine that prolongeth life
items.note: The margin note says how the life-prolonging medicine is got: the purified Elements are brought to a pure and equal simplicity. No step of work is given beyond this.

items.quote: the inequality and dominion of one over another is it that breedeth diseases
items.note: The note's reason: diseases are bred by one Element ruling over another.

items.quote: Mans health consisteth in the agreement and union of the Three First Substances
items.note: Health is the agreement and union of the Three First Substances.

items.quote: when they are exalted and set on fire by the Stars, the intestine wars follow
items.note: Sickness is put as inward war that follows when the three are 'exalted' and set on fire by the Stars.

items.quote: they give place to the Essence of Fire which consumeth the disease and separateth the pure from the impure
items.note: The three substances of diseases, called 'valitile' just before, yield to the Essence of Fire, which consumes the disease and parts pure from impure.

items.quote: Health consisteth in a Temperate body.
items.note: The margin note puts the paragraph's opening in other words: health is a temperate body.

items.quote: as the celestiall Sun hardneth the Clay and softneth the Wax
items.note: The margin note says one act of one thing differs according to what receives it, with the Sun hardening clay and softening wax as its example.

items.quote: that Fift Essence of the Human Body bindeth the Elements or Humors in Peace and Harmonicall league, and reduceth to the true Temperament by making equall the unequall
items.note: Here the text speaks of a Fift Essence 'of the Human Body' and says it binds the Elements or Humors in peace and restores the temperament by making the unequal equal.

items.quote: so long as the Radicall Humor, the Vitall Balsom and most precious Nectar of our Life abideth in its quantity, we are not sensible of any disease
items.note: Three names stand together for one thing (Radicall Humor, Vitall Balsom, Nectar of our Life); while its quantity holds, no disease is felt.

items.quote: the strengthning power of the Human body and of Animalls proceedeth from the spirit of Life
items.note: The strength of the body, in man and beast, is said to come from the spirit of Life.

items.quote: even to his Naturall death, that is to that Terme of Life which the Omnipotent God hath appointed to Man for disobedience
items.note: The text says what it means by natural death: the term of life God set for man because of disobedience. The medicine is said to keep a man sound up to that term, not beyond it.

items.quote: such a man who shall use it prudently and seasonably with a devout calling upon the Name of the Lord
items.note: Conditions on the user: prudent and timely use with devout prayer; just before the text speaks of 'the predisposed or fore-qualified Man', and just after it adds a proviso about the body's constitution (a word there is partly unreadable).

items.quote: this Fift Essence and Spirituall Medicine, which hath the Nature and Heat of Heaven (not of our mortall and corruptible)
items.what: this Fift Essence and Spirituall Medicine
items.note: The Fift Essence is named a Spirituall Medicine, with the nature and heat of Heaven and not of the mortal and corruptible kind.

items.quote: it is possible to find out the True Fonntaine of Physick, the Conservation of Life, the Restitution of health, the Renovation of lost youth, and the desired clear health
items.note: What Croll says can be found in it: the true fountain of physic, preservation of life, restoring of health, renewal of lost youth.

items.quote: and to speak Naturally
items.note: The author marks the claim that follows as spoken 'Naturally'; the phrase sets this way of speaking apart from another, which these words do not name.

items.quote: there is no Balsamick Medicine in all the world better than this true Triacle of Phylosophers, which like the Elixir of life is the superlative and last consolation of Mans body
items.note: The medicine is named the true Triacle of Phylosophers and likened to the Elixir of life.

items.quote: For in every kind there is a certaine One that holdeth the first degree in that kind
items.note: A general ground Croll gives: every kind has one member that holds first rank in it.

items.quote: this Medicine is made of the more incorruptible and efficacious Matter that can be under Heaven, that is, the Soule or Spirit of the world, which hath in it the force of all Celestiall and Terrestriall things
items.note: The text says what the medicine's matter is: the Soule or Spirit of the world, which holds the force of all heavenly and earthly things.

items.quote: it ought to hold the first degree in the order of Physick, and the Man that useth it with the moderation of other meat, may live as long as the ancient Fathers
items.note: Croll ranks it first in physic and says a man who uses it, with moderation in other food, may live as long as the ancient Fathers.

items.quote: The Heat of the Sun and Moon is that Naturall Heat whereby every thing is digested for the sustentation and multiplication of
items.note: The margin note equates the Heat of the Sun and Moon with the natural heat by which everything is digested (the last word of the sentence has an unreadable letter).

items.quote: The Spirit is the life and Balsom of all Naturall things.
items.note: The note says what the Spirit is: the life and Balsom of all natural things.

items.quote: From those two fountaines the SUN and MOON, as Suchtenius learnedly discourseth, springeth the Naturall and Vitall Spirit of the world, which runneth thorow all Beings, giving life and consistance to all things
items.name: Suchtenius
items.note: The teaching that the natural and vital Spirit of the world springs from Sun and Moon is given with the name of Suchtenius, with approval. Where his words end the text does not show.

items.quote: there can be nothing in all the world that may or can be without a spark of this Spirit
items.note: Nothing in the world is without a spark of this Spirit; the sentence is the one that names Suchtenius, so whose words these are is not marked.

items.quote: This Celestiall Spirit which is one and the same with our Naturall spirit, when its breathing in our body is not lesned or hindred by outward things, is that Naturall Heat of ours
items.note: The Celestiall Spirit is said to be one with our natural spirit, and, when unhindered in the body, to be our natural heat.

items.quote: It digesteth the nourishment that Man taketh, and breeds good blood in all the members
items.note: The work of this heat in the body: it digests food and breeds good blood; the text goes on to say that hindered by sickness it concocts badly, breeds bad blood and weakens the vital spirit of the heart.

items.quote: at last followeth a full extinction, consumption and dissipation of that spirit, which is the Naturall Death
items.note: Here natural death is said to be the full going out and scattering of that spirit, following old age.

items.quote: that spirit and Naturall Heat in Humane bodies so weakned and hindred must be increased and strengthned, that it may be the better able to do its duty
items.note: The remedy Croll states: the weakened spirit and natural heat must be increased and strengthened; the same sentence limits the prevention with 'as much as by Nature may be'.

items.quote: The Life of Man is the Astral Balsom. the Balsamick Impression, the Celestiall and Invisible Fire, the Aire shut up, and the Tincturing Spirit of Salt.
items.note: The margin note says what the life of man is, in five names set side by side.

items.quote: every agent when it begins to act, doth not move toward any thing below it selfe, but to that which is equall like and sutable to it
items.note: The ground for what follows: an agent acts toward what is equal and like to it, not toward what is below it.

items.quote: this strengthning also must be by its like, that is, by that Celestiall Heat of the Sun and Moon, and the other Planets
items.note: The strengthening must be by a like thing, which the text names: the celestial heat of Sun, Moon and the other planets; or, it goes on, things in which the virtue of Sun and Moon is strongest or least held back by matter.

items.quote: the spirit or that supernall Fire is got out of them by art
items.note: The one step of work named here: the spirit, or supernal Fire, is got out of such things by art, and more easily from them. How is not said in these lines.

items.quote: burning Heat, consuming all things, and darknesse, making all things barren, are proper to the Elementall and Inferior Fire
items.note: The text sets two fires apart: burning heat and darkness belong to the Elementall and Inferior Fire; just before, heat that does not burn but makes fruitful, and life-giving light, are said to belong to the supernal Fire.

items.quote: The Celestiall or that Spirit of the world and the Naturall Spirit of our body is one and the same Spirit
items.note: The margin note states that the Spirit of the world and the natural spirit of our body are one and the same.

items.quote: That same (Heat) therefore is excluded, as also with it all divers and contrary things, such as are all the inferior Elements
items.note: The elemental heat, and with it the inferior Elements, are shut out as means of strengthening; the word 'Heat' stands in brackets in the text.

items.quote: all things else that include a Naturall composition in them (so far as they are yet drowned in a thick grosse matter, and as yet not separate from it) are subject to corruption and transmutation
items.note: Compounded things are open to corruption so far as they are still sunk in gross matter and not separated from it; the bracket makes the separation the point on which this turns.

items.quote: Medicines ought to be preserving and very durable, and remote from corruption
items.note: What a medicine must be: lasting and far from corruption, since otherwise it would corrupt the body rather than preserve it.

items.quote: tis but in vaine to think to preserve a corruptible body by a putrid and corruptible thing, to cure the weak by a feeble thing
items.note: A corruptible body cannot be preserved by a corruptible thing, nor the weak cured by a feeble thing.

items.quote: Every corruptible weak and feeble thing added to its like, augmenteth it
items.note: The rule behind it: a corruptible thing added to its like increases it.

items.quote: too many Physitians of our time who labor in vaine to cure Men of their maladies by their grosse and corporall compositions of Medicines
items.note: Croll's charge against physicians of his time: they work in vain with gross, bodily compounded medicines.

items.quote: but a higher speculation is here required
items.note: The author says this matter asks for a higher kind of consideration than the bodily one just named.

items.quote: whereas diseases are not corporall, but spirituall and lurking in the spirits, they also call for spirituall medicines
items.note: Diseases are said to be spiritual and seated in the spirits, and so to need spiritual medicines.

items.quote: One Like added to its like maketh it more Like.
items.note: The margin note gives the rule of the paragraph as a short saying.

items.quote: The vitall spirit in Man & the Elemental is one spirit.
items.note: This margin note calls the vital spirit in man one with 'the Elemental'; the paragraphs around it set the Elementall against the Celestiall and tell the reader to seek 'not the Elementall', and the note to CH6.57 makes the spirit of our body one with the Celestiall. The two do not agree as worded; it rests on the single word 'Elemental'.

items.quote: that vitall spirit (which is the Radicall Moysture and Heat
items.note: A bracket says what the vital spirit is: the Radicall Moysture and Heat.

items.quote: the innate Mummy, and hath its seat in the midst of Mans heart, as the sustentacle of all our life
items.note: The same bracket goes on: it is the innate Mummy, seated in the midst of the heart, the support of all our life.

items.quote: they must seek after not the Elementall, but that Celestiall Heat of the Sun and Moon that dwelleth in the more incorruptible substance that is to be found under the Globe of the Moon
items.note: Those who would preserve and repair the vital spirit must seek the celestial heat of Sun and Moon, which dwells in the more incorruptible substance found under the moon; the substance is not named in these lines.

items.quote: to make this like our heart or spirit, which is done, when it is prepared and made up into a medicine and most pleasant meat, so that being taken by the mouth
items.note: The work named: the thing is made like our heart or spirit by being prepared and made up into a medicine and pleasant food, taken by mouth; the text then lists what it does in the body. No steps of the preparing are given.

items.quote: This is the duty of a true Physitian, and of the more sound Phylosopher.
items.note: Croll calls this seeking and preparing the duty of the true physician and sounder philosopher.

items.quote: The Innate Heat and Radical Moysture of the Microcosm are sustained by the MacrocoMacrocosmicall Heat and Moysture of the Sun and Moon
items.note: The margin note says the inborn heat and moisture of the Microcosm are upheld by the heat and moisture of Sun and Moon in the greater world (the word is printed doubled).

items.quote: retard old age, keep youth flourishing in its vigour to the very poynt of death
items.note: What such a physician could do: hold back old age and keep youth in vigour up to the point of death.

items.quote: were it not for the wages of sin, withstand death, preserve (our body) in perpetuall health and defend it from destruction
items.note: The limit Croll sets: death itself would be withstood but for 'the wages of sin'.

items.quote: The Tincture doth so cleanse the Balsom, that our children in the tenth generation may see the effect of it living so long, Paracels.
items.name: Paracels.
items.note: The margin note gives a saying under the name 'Paracels.': the Tincture cleanses the Balsom so that the effect is seen to the tenth generation.

items.quote: Paracelsus calleth it the Element of FIRE, which like the Sun of the Terrene or inferiour Firmament may be the greatest Secret for the removing all diseases
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: A name for the thing is given to Paracelsus: the Element of FIRE; it is likened to a sun of the lower firmament and called the greatest secret for removing diseases.

items.quote: that Essentiall Fire worketh in the body, as the Flame and Nettle doth without the body
items.note: How the fire works: inside the body as flame and nettle work on its outside.

items.quote: Whose meaning was (that of right he may here be vindicated from the unjust calumny wherewith he was branded)
items.note: Croll announces that he is giving what Paracelsus meant, in order to clear him of a calumny; what follows is offered as the right sense of Paracelsus's words on the 'perfect Fire of Life'.

items.quote: the Balsamick Mummy, the Vitall Body, the liquor of Life, the Native or Radicall Humor which the Spirit of Life moveth or acteth, may be restor'd, strengthned and preserved
items.note: The meaning Croll gives: the thing named by this run of names (with 'the Balsom of Nature' just before) may be restored, strengthened and preserved.

items.quote: even to the very utmost consumption of it, that is, to the last gasp of Life without any sicknesse, paine and griefe
items.note: The reach of that preserving: to the last breath of life, without sickness or pain; not beyond it.

items.quote: being Poysoned in his body by his malicious and inhuman adversaries, who had often attempted the same before they could effect it
items.note: Croll says Paracelsus was stopped from his cures by being poisoned by adversaries.

items.quote: he came to the Naturall Terme of his Life by an untimely and violent death of a draught of Poyson
items.note: The death by poison is called both untimely and violent and the coming to the 'Naturall Terme of his Life'; it rests on the wording of that phrase.

items.quote: that he by this his medicine would presumptously prepare himselfe an entrance and way to the immortall health of his body
items.name: many
items.note: A charge reported in order to reject it, given to 'many' who 'maliciously scoffe in their strange fictions': that Paracelsus meant by his medicine to make his body immortal.

items.quote: The Humors of life do nourish the spirit of life.
items.note: The margin note beside the run of names says the humors of life feed the spirit of life.

items.quote: See Paracel. in the sift Tome among his Physicall fragments, sol. 162.
items.name: Paracel.
items.note: The margin note names a writing of Paracelsus and a place in it beside the passage that gives his meaning.

items.quote: Cease therefore henceforth to blame Paracelsus in that he promisedlong life to others, but scarce came to full age himselfe.
items.note: The note names the blame it rejects: that Paracelsus promised long life to others and scarcely reached full age himself; it adds that such things are devised out of 'malicious ignorance'.

items.quote: GOD is the Centre of all Creatures, by how much the more any draw near to him, by so much the more blessed, and lesse variable, and mutable is he
items.note: God is the centre of all creatures; the nearer to him, the more blessed and the less changeable.

items.quote: that Centre or One, to wit, the immutable will of God
items.note: The text says what the Centre or One is: the unchangeable will of God; against it stand the circumference, variety and plurality of the creatures.

items.quote: Blessednesse is in unity, not in the circumference; in Christ, not in the world, is Peace and the Rest of Soules.
items.note: Blessedness is placed in unity and in Christ, not in the circumference or the world.

items.quote: He that continueth united with God in Christ doth like God and the Angels never wax old.
items.note: The margin note says that one who stays united with God in Christ never grows old, like God and the Angels.

items.quote: In vaine will those husks & scraps of Paracelsus rise up that use to do, who exclaime that this interpretation is forced and far setch'd.
items.note: The note calls what stands beside it 'this interpretation' and expects some, whom it calls husks and scraps of Paracelsus, to cry that it is forced; it rejects their cry beforehand.

items.quote: shall forget all Things and leave sensible and Temporall things behind him, which are to be used but onely in our passage, and shall be united to that one Centre
items.note: The way named: to forget all things, leave behind the things of sense and time, which are only for use on the way, and be united to the one Centre.

items.quote: he waxeth young rather than old: And this is the true Long Life of the Cabalists, and of Paracelsus
items.note: The text itself says what 'the true Long Life' is: the growing young of one united to the Centre. Earlier paragraphs given here (CH6.55, CH6.60–61) speak of long life of the body by the medicine.

items.quote: which he so often and so earnestly begg'd for by Prayer and holy hope in his Hymns and Soliloquies, the true Enochean Life
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: Paracelsus is said to have begged for this life in prayer in his Hymns and Soliloquies; it is given a further name, the true Enochean Life.

items.quote: he that is not united to this most united Fountain-like and only Unity by adhaesion, must of necessity perish for ever, and be separated from the Light and Life by the second death
items.note: The contrary case: one not united to the Unity by 'adhaesion' perishes for ever and is parted from Light and Life by the second death.

items.quote: which deprivation and want of the sight of God is the most bitter of all punishments
items.note: Being without the sight of God is called the bitterest of punishments.

items.quote: To know GOD himselfe the maker of all things, and passe into him with a full image of his likenesse, as with a kind of essentiall touch without a bond
items.note: What is to be sought: to know God and pass into him with a full image of his likeness, as by an 'essentiall touch'.

items.quote: whereby thou mayest be transform'd, and made (as it were) a God, this at last will prove the True and sollid Phylosophy
items.note: The text says what the true and solid Phylosophy is: this knowing and passing into God, by which one is transformed and made, with the guard 'as it were', a God.

items.quote: The MIND therefore of Adept Phylosophers, whose
items.note: The text sets apart a group, the Adept Phylosophers, and their MIND, printed in capitals; the word that follows is in a foreign script the transcription leaves out, glossed 'or conversation is in Heaven'.

items.quote: to whom one is All in all, and All are one in One
items.note: Of these philosophers: for them one is all in all, and all are one in One.

items.quote: who alwayes look upon these transitory things with the left eye, but on Heaven with the right
items.note: A figure of two eyes: the left for passing things, the right for Heaven.

items.quote: Phil. 3.20.
items.name: Phil. 3.20.
items.note: The margin note names a place of scripture beside the words on a conversation in Heaven.

items.quote: The Mystery of Divine Matrimony with Man.
items.what: The Mystery of Divine Matrimony with Man
items.note: The margin note heads the passage as a mystery: a divine marriage with man.

items.quote: of these Adept Phylosophers hath ever been far off and estranged from the Cavill above mentioned
items.note: Points back to a cavil named earlier; in the lines given, CH6.62 reports the scoff that Paracelsus sought immortal health of the body. The mind of the Adept Phylosophers is said to be far from it.

items.quote: they have by a quiet and religious meditation been raised up out of the sepulchre of their body or out of the dead Works of Darknesse
items.note: A raising from a grave is spoken of in the living: the 'sepulchre' is their body, or the dead works of darkness, and the raising is by meditation with grace.

items.quote: be turned to God in the Sabbath of their Heart by a separation of the Minde from Terrene obsticles in themselves
items.note: The turning to God is by a separation of the mind from earthly hindrances within; 'separation' is here said of the mind.

items.quote: one simple (intuitive vision or) sight from within, a kind of an Essentiall touch of the Divinity
items.note: After 'to wit' the text says what seeing all things in one is: one simple sight from within, a kind of essential touch of the Divinity.

items.quote: which beauty is incomprehensible to the Old Creature
items.note: The beauty of the Chiefest Good, seen in the light of God, is said to be beyond the grasp of 'the Old Creature'.

items.quote: to stay so long in this Vale of miseries and ignorance
items.note: These philosophers are said to count it unhappiness to stay so long in this vale; the margin sets the Latin word INFORTUNIUM beside it.

items.quote: the most beautifull Nothing (that is, the shadow and region of Darknesse and Death)
items.note: A bracket says what 'the most beautifull Nothing' is: the shadow and region of darkness and death, to be cast behind.

items.quote: returned to the BEING of BEINGS (from whom we are wandred) as to the prefixed scope of all our desires and will
items.note: The heart has no rest until it returns to the BEING of BEINGS, the set aim of all desire.

items.quote: they leave themselves, and totally go out from themselves contemning all things corporeall and incorporeall
items.note: They are said to leave and go out from themselves, setting at nought all things bodily and unbodily, and hasten from the imperfect to the one and perfect.

items.quote: the most wise Hermes and most pious Phylosopher of reverend antiquity the Antesignan of Naturall Phylosophers and first Prophet
items.note: Hermes is named with a run of titles: most wise, most pious philosopher of antiquity, foremost of natural philosophers, first prophet.

items.quote: doth also acknowledge in his Monade) is a sacred, Heavenly, and hid silence, the quiet or Rest of the sences and all things
items.name: Hermes
items.note: Hermes, in a writing called 'his Monade', is said to acknowledge the same; the knowledge and contemplation of the one and perfect is called a sacred, heavenly and hid silence, the rest of the senses.

items.quote: all minds, by an unanimous friendship, after an unutterable manner, shall be altogether but one thing, in one MIND which is above every MIND
items.note: At the end of labours all minds shall be one thing in one MIND above every mind, in a way that cannot be spoken.

items.quote: It is the intimate vision of GOD, and the Intuitive knowledge of GOD, which also hapneth by the Light of Grace to the separate Soul even in this world
items.note: The text says what this is: the inward vision and intuitive knowledge of God, which by the Light of Grace also comes to 'the separate Soul' in this world, on conditions named next.

items.quote: Thus many holy men by vertue of the Deifick Spirit have tasted the First fruits of the Resurrection in this life
items.note: Many holy men are said to have tasted the first fruits of the Resurrection in this life.

items.quote: I mean that spirituall Death of the Saints (which the Jewes call the kisse of Death) which is precious in the sight of God
items.name: the Jewes
items.note: The author says what he means, a spiritual death of the Saints, and gives a name for it to 'the Jewes': the kisse of Death.

items.quote: if the fulnesse of Life may be called death
items.note: The author says the word death is not meant plainly here: what he calls death is the fulness of life.

items.quote: We must die to the World, Flesh, Blood, and the whole Animall Man, who would faine have got into those Inmost secrets, and entred into Paradise by the excesse or going out of the MIND
items.note: The 'Inmost secrets' are open only to those who die to world, flesh, blood and the whole 'Animall Man'; the entry is by the 'excesse or going out of the MIND'.

items.quote: the Man that liveth in nothing but the Mind, is as an Angel
items.note: One who lives only in the Mind is as an Angel and, the text adds with a guard, takes in God after a sort.

items.quote: not after the Limus Terrae the Eearthy Mind
items.note: The Latin words Limus Terrae are set beside 'the Eearthy Mind'; the friends of God live after the image or inspiration of the most High and not after this.

items.quote: who from Divine Love willingly cast themselves headlong into the fountaine of the Abysse and into the Sea of Nihilitude or Nothingnesse, and enter into the Holies of Holies by the Life of Christ
items.note: The friends of God cast themselves, out of divine love, into the Abysse and the Sea of Nihilitude or Nothingnesse, and enter the Holies of Holies by the Life of Christ.

items.quote: the Sea of Nihilitude or Nothingnesse
items.note: Earlier in this paragraph 'Nothing' is the shadow and region of darkness and death, to be cast behind, and the margin says whatever is not God is Nothing; here the friends of God cast themselves into 'Nothingnesse' on the way to God. The word is used of two unlike things; it rests on the one word.

items.quote: By the Soul abiding and standing stedfast, embracing its Image of Divinity or MIND united to GOD by Christ, we enjoy actuall Blessednesse.
items.note: The closing sentence of the lines given sets 'Image of Divinity' beside MIND as names of one thing, and says actual blessedness is enjoyed when the soul holds fast to it, united to God by Christ.

items.quote: By the access of this beam, ray, or celestiall Stone all drosse is purified, and the darknesse of ignorance is driven away.
items.note: The margin note beside the MIND of the Adept Phylosophers speaks of a 'celestiall Stone' set side by side with a beam or ray, and of purifying dross together with driving away ignorance.

items.name: Eccl. 18.9, 10. Psal. 90.10. Rom. 8.
items.note: Places of scripture named in the margin beside the opening of the paragraph.

items.quote: Whatsoever is not God, is Nothing, and ought to be esteemed as nothing.
items.note: The margin note says what Nothing is: whatever is not God.

items.quote: INFORTUNIUM.
items.note: A single Latin word in capitals set in the margin beside the words on the unhappiness of staying in this vale.

items.quote: Lactantias mentioneth Hermes not so much among the Naturall Phylosophers, as among the Sybylis and Prophets, as the true Orpheus.
items.name: Lactantias
items.note: The margin note cites Lactantias for counting Hermes among the Sibyls and Prophets rather than among the natural philosophers.

items.quote: All things are seen and lookt into with one presentiall glance.
items.note: The margin note beside the vision of God: all things are seen in one present glance.

items.name: Exod. 33. Es. 6. 2 Cor. 11. Psal. 116.15.
items.note: Places of scripture named in the margin beside the spiritual death of the Saints that is 'precious in the sight of God'.
